implementation_notes: JavaScript has no `goto`, no labelled loops and no tail calls, so exceptions are the only universal control-flow construct — which means JavaScript programmers reach for them when they need a multi-level exit, and that is the canonical modern spaghetti. The other JavaScript-specific tangle is `async`: deeply nested `await` inside callbacks, promise chains whose error paths are `catch` at the end of a chain nobody can follow, and mixing `async` functions with `then` chains so the control flow alternates between two models. Linting for `no-throw-literal`, complexity thresholds, and a hard rule that a thrown control-flow exception type is private to its own module are the practical guards.
idiom_name: exception-as-break; nested ternaries; async control flow
pitfalls: Throwing non-Error values makes control flow indistinguishable from failure.
`Promise.all` rejection order plus a shared `.catch` at the end makes error attribution depend on which promise lost the race.
A `try` wrapping an `await` inside a `forEach` swallows rejections because `forEach` does not await the returned promises — a silent control-flow bug.
